doctrines/angels-spiritual-powers/questi: What are angels and demons, and how should the church engage the spiritual powers?
doctrines/angels-spiritual-powers/summar: Christians have always confessed God as Creator of things visible and invisible, but have differed over the ordering of angels, the origin of demons, the practice of exorcism and deliverance, whether the “powers” are personal spirits, social structures or myth — and have had to reckon with the witch-hunts that demonology helped to fuel.
doctrines/angels-spiritual-powers/longTe:
The Bible is full of angels — seraphim around the throne, Michael and the “prince of Persia”, the angels who guard the little ones — and the gospels show Jesus casting out demons and announcing Satan’s fall. Second Temple Judaism had elaborated these themes, notably in the Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch), still canonical in the Ethiopian church, which traced demons to angels who sinned with human women. Early Christian writers such as Justin and Tertullian followed it; Origen and especially Augustine instead taught that Satan and the demons were angels who fell through pride, and the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) confessed that the devil was created good. Desert monks such as Antony and Evagrius made the discernment of demonic “thoughts” a pillar of spirituality, and baptismal exorcisms and the renunciation of Satan entered the liturgy of every ancient church.

Around 500 the anonymous Pseudo-Dionysius arranged the angels into nine orders in three triads, an angelology that shaped Gregory the Great, Aquinas (the “Angelic Doctor”), Dante and Gothic art; guardian angels became a beloved devotion, with a universal feast from 1670. The Reformers kept a vivid sense of the devil — “our ancient foe” — but criticised exorcism rites and speculative angelology.

The darkest chapter is the early modern witch-hunt. Fusing scholastic demonology with heresy trials and misogyny, the Malleus Maleficarum (1486) presented witchcraft as a female conspiracy with Satan; Catholic and Protestant courts executed perhaps 40,000-60,000 people, most of them women, before sceptics such as Friedrich Spee, Alonso de Salazar, Balthasar Bekker and Increase Mather helped end the trials; Salem (1692) became the emblem of moral panic. Bekker’s denial of the devil’s power foreshadowed Enlightenment and liberal scepticism, culminating in Bultmann’s call (1941) to demythologise the New Testament spirit world. Walter Wink proposed a third way: the powers are the spiritual interiority of institutions, disarmed by Christ’s cross.

Meanwhile Christianity’s centre of gravity shifted to the Global South, where spirits, ancestors and witchcraft are lived realities. African prophets such as William Wade Harris, the Aladura and Pentecostal churches, Ethiopian holy-water ministries and Catholic healers such as Archbishop Milingo proclaimed Christ’s victory over the powers; Pentecostal and charismatic deliverance ministry spread worldwide; and in the 1990s C. Peter Wagner’s “strategic-level spiritual warfare” against territorial spirits drew warnings from the Lausanne movement and cessationist critics. The Catholic Church revised its rite of exorcism in 1999, requiring medical discernment, and churches in Africa and the Pacific now struggle both to minister deliverance and to stop witchcraft accusations against the vulnerable.
doctrines/angels-spiritual-powers/flow/n: What are angels and demons, and how should Christians engage the spiritual powers?

The Bible speaks of angels, Satan, demons and “principalities and powers”. Are they personal beings, structures, or myth? How did evil spirits arise? How should the church deliver the afflicted — and how did beliefs about the devil lead to the horrors of the witch-hunts?
Isaiah 6; Daniel 10; Psalm 91:11; Matthew 18:10; Hebrews 1:14

Seraphim cry “Holy, holy, holy”; the “prince of Persia” withstands Michael; “he shall give his angels charge over thee”; “their angels do always behold the face of my Father”; angels are “ministering spirits”. (Daniel is usually dated to the 2nd century BC.)
Genesis 6:1-4 and 1 Enoch 6-16 (Book of the Watchers)
“The sons of God saw the daughters of men …”. The Book of the Watchers, canonical in the Ethiopian church and quoted in Jude 14-15, tells of angels who descended and corrupted humanity.
Mark 1:21-28; 5:1-20; Luke 10:17-20; Ephesians 6:10-18; Colossians 2:15

Jesus casts out unclean spirits; “I beheld Satan as lightning fall from heaven”; “we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers”; Christ “spoiled principalities and powers … triumphing over them”.
Early Christians adopt the Watchers story
Justin, Athenagoras, Irenaeus and Tertullian explain demons as offspring of fallen Watchers.
Origen: rational beings fall by degrees
Origen locates Satan’s fall in free choice and speculates that all rational creatures, perhaps even demons, may be restored.
Antony and the desert fathers: the monk as spiritual warrior
The Life of Antony and later Evagrius make discernment of demonic thoughts central to Christian spirituality.
Baptismal exorcisms and the Church’s prayers
Cyril of Jerusalem and Chrysostom describe exorcisms and renunciation of Satan in baptism — practices continued in Orthodox, Oriental and Catholic rites.
Augustine: angels fell through pride
City of God sets the classic Western account and rejects the angelic-marriage reading of Genesis 6.
Constantinople II rejects the restoration of demons (553)
Anathemas associated with the council condemn Origenist teachings, including the pre-existence of souls and final restoration of demons.
Pseudo-Dionysius: the celestial hierarchy
Nine orders of angels in three triads mediating divine light.
Gregory the Great transmits the nine orders to the West
Gregory’s homilies and Dialogues popularise angelology and stories of demonic temptation.
John of Damascus defines the angels
A concise Eastern synthesis: angels are incorporeal, free, immortal by grace; the devil fell by his own choice.
Fourth Lateran: the devil was created good (1215)
Against Cathar dualism, the council confesses that the devil and other demons were created naturally good by God but became evil by their own doing.
Aquinas, the “Angelic Doctor”
Aquinas’ treatise on angels systematises their nature, knowledge, fall and ministry, including guardian angels.
Witch-hunting demonology and the Malleus (1486)
Scholastic demonology fused with heresy trials and misogyny to produce the theory of a satanic witch sect — a development all churches now repudiate.
Luther: “our ancient foe”
The Reformers kept a vivid sense of the devil while rejecting many Catholic exorcism rites as superstitious.
Rituale Romanum regulates exorcism (1614)
Paul V’s ritual standardises solemn exorcism and its cautions for nearly four centuries.
Spee’s Cautio Criminalis: torture creates witches
A Jesuit confessor of condemned witches exposes the injustice of the trials.
Guardian angels: feast made universal (1670)
Clement X extends the feast of the Guardian Angels to the whole Latin Church, crowning a long patristic and scholastic tradition.
Bekker’s The World Bewitched (1691)
A Dutch Reformed minister denies that the devil can act in the physical world — and is deposed.
Salem witch trials (1692)
Twenty people die in Puritan Massachusetts before ministers’ objections to spectral evidence end the trials.
African prophets confront the spirit powers
William Wade Harris burns fetishes and baptises tens of thousands; Kimbangu, the Aladura churches and later African Pentecostals proclaim Christ’s power over spirits and witchcraft.
Cessationism: the sign-gifts have ceased
Warfield’s Counterfeit Miracles grounds a Reformed critique of later deliverance ministries.
Bultmann: demythologising the spirit world
Bultmann argues that modern people cannot believe in spirits and demons and must interpret them existentially.
C. S. Lewis: two equal and opposite errors
The Screwtape Letters reaffirms personal devils for a sceptical age while warning against fascination with them.
Pentecostal and charismatic deliverance ministry
Derek Prince and others teach that believers can be “demonised” and freed through deliverance.
Wink: the powers as the spirit of institutions
A third way between supernaturalism and demythologising, linked to Christus Victor and nonviolence.
Strategic-level spiritual warfare
Wagner, Otis and others teach mapping and binding territorial spirits; it feeds into the New Apostolic Reformation.
Lausanne statement on spiritual warfare (1993)
Evangelical leaders affirm spiritual warfare but warn against speculative mapping and animistic thinking.
Revised Catholic Rite of Exorcism (1999)
The new rite requires medical and psychiatric discernment before solemn exorcism.
Cessationist critique: Strange Fire (2013)
John MacArthur and others charge that charismatic warfare techniques depart from the sufficiency of Scripture.
Deliverance and witchcraft accusations in the Global South

Deliverance ministry is central to African, Latin American and Asian Christianity; churches and theologians also campaign against witchcraft accusations targeting children, widows and the elderly in parts of Africa and Papua New Guinea.
Today

Catholic dioceses appoint more exorcists and Pope Francis insists the devil is personal; Orthodox and Ethiopian churches maintain ancient practices; Pentecostals and charismatics practise deliverance worldwide; Western academic theology largely follows Bultmann or Wink; and cessationists and critics of NAR warn against excess.
doctrines/covenant-law/question: How do the old and new covenants relate, and what becomes of Israel, the Law and the Sabbath?
doctrines/covenant-law/summary: From the Council of Jerusalem and Marcion to the Reformation’s law–gospel debates, Westminster covenant theology, dispensationalism, theonomy and post-Holocaust rethinking, Christians have argued over how Christ fulfils the covenants with Israel, what the Law of Moses still requires, and which day is holy.
doctrines/covenant-law/longText:
Christianity began as a movement within Judaism. Its first great decision, at Jerusalem around AD 49, freed Gentile believers from circumcision and the full Law of Moses, while Jewish believers went on keeping it. Within a century the church was overwhelmingly Gentile. Marcion tried to cut the Hebrew Scriptures away altogether, and the church answered through Irenaeus that one God gave both covenants. Justin and others called the church "the true spiritual Israel". This fulfilment or supersessionist reading became the consensus of East and West. In its harsher forms it fed a long "teaching of contempt" that ran from Chrysostom’s sermons to crusader massacres, Lateran IV’s legislation, expulsions and Luther’s late tracts.

The Reformation reopened the question of the Law. Luther made the distinction between law and gospel the key to preaching. When his colleague Agricola concluded that the law has no place among the justified, Luther and Melanchthon replied that the law still convicts and, in Melanchthon’s "third use", guides the regenerate. In Zurich, Bullinger read the whole Bible as one covenant of grace. Reformed theologians added a pre-fall covenant of works, and the Westminster Confession (1647) codified federal theology: the ceremonial law is abrogated, the judicial law has expired except for its "general equity", the moral law binds all, and the Lord’s Day is "the Christian Sabbath". Disputes followed over antinomianism in Massachusetts (1637) and over the Marrow of Modern Divinity in Scotland (1718–23). The fourth commandment divided Puritan Sabbatarians, continental Protestants and Catholics, and later Seventh Day Baptists and Seventh-day Adventists, who kept the seventh day as the Ethiopian church had long honoured it. The medieval compulsory tithe, first enforced at Mâcon (585), survives as voluntary tithing in many churches.

In the 19th century J. N. Darby’s dispensationalism separated Israel and the church and expected a literal national restoration. Through the Scofield Reference Bible it shaped American evangelicalism and Christian Zionism. Rushdoony’s theonomy (1973) pressed the continuing civil force of Mosaic law, and most Reformed churches rejected it. Progressive dispensationalism, New Covenant Theology and progressive covenantalism looked for middle ways. The Shoah forced a deeper reckoning. Nostra Aetate (1965) rejected the deicide charge, and many churches have since repudiated punitive supersessionism. Theologians now debate fulfilment, two-covenant and bilateral models, and Messianic Jews claim a Jewish way of following Jesus. This section sets out each view in its own terms, with its strongest critics.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/0/labe: How do the old and new covenants relate, and what becomes of Israel, the Law and the Sabbath?
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/0/text: Jesus was a Jew who said he came "not to destroy, but to fulfil" the Law; Paul declared that Christ is "the end of the law" yet that the law is "holy". Has the Church replaced Israel, joined it, or does Israel keep its own covenant? Does the Law of Moses still bind Christians — its moral, ceremonial or civil parts — and what of the Sabbath and the tithe?
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/1/labe: Abraham, Sinai and the promised new covenant (Gen 15; 17; Exod 19–24; Jer 31:31–34)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/1/text: God covenants with Abraham and his seed, gives Israel the Law at Sinai with the Sabbath as its sign (Exod 31:13–17), and through Jeremiah promises "a new covenant" with the law written on the heart. Tithes support the Levites and the poor (Lev 27:30; Deut 14; Mal 3:8–10). Every later system is an attempt to say how these covenants fit together.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/2/labe: "Not to destroy, but to fulfil" (Matt 5:17–19; Mark 2:27–28; Matt 23:23)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/2/text: Jesus affirms that not one jot of the Law will pass "till all be fulfilled", calls himself "Lord also of the sabbath", and commends tithing while rebuking neglect of "judgment, mercy, and faith". Readers dispute whether "fulfil" means confirm, complete or bring to an end.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/3/labe: Paul on the Law and Israel (Gal 3–4; Rom 7; 9–11; 2 Cor 3)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/3/text: The Law was a "schoolmaster" until Christ (Gal 3:24); "Christ is the end of the law for righteousness" (Rom 10:4), yet "the law is holy" (Rom 7:12) and "all Israel shall be saved", for "the gifts and calling of God are without repentance" (Rom 11:26–29). Gentiles are grafted into Israel’s olive tree (Rom 11:17–24).
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/4/labe: Hebrews and Colossians: shadow and substance (Heb 8:6–13; 10:1; Col 2:16–17)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/4/text: "In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old" (Heb 8:13); the Law has "a shadow of good things to come"; Christians are not to be judged "in respect of an holyday ... or of the sabbath days". Hebrews 7 also reads Abraham’s tithe to Melchizedek christologically.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/5/labe: Council of Jerusalem: Gentiles not bound to circumcision (c.49)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/5/text: The apostles and elders decide that Gentile believers need not be circumcised or keep the whole Law, asking only abstention from idol-food, blood, things strangled and sexual immorality (Acts 15). Jewish believers continue to keep the Law for a generation or more.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/6/text: Ignatius contrasts Judaizing with living "in the observance of the Lord’s Day"; Justin (c.155) describes Christians assembling "on the day called Sunday". The first day, the day of resurrection, becomes the Christian day of worship.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/7/labe: Marcion: two Gods, no Old Testament (c.144)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/7/text: Marcion sets the just Creator-God of the Law against the good Father revealed by Jesus, rejects the Hebrew Scriptures and edits Luke and Paul. The Roman church expels him (144); his challenge forces the church to affirm one God of both covenants and to define its canon.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/8/labe: Justin: the Church as "the true spiritual Israel" (c.155)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/8/text: In the Dialogue with Trypho, Justin argues that Christians, not the Jews who reject Jesus, are the heirs of Israel’s promises, and that the Law was given because of Israel’s hardness of heart: an early and influential form of supersessionism.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/9/labe: Supersession / fulfilment: the Church as the new Israel (2nd c.)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/9/text: From Barnabas, Justin and Melito onwards, the dominant view holds that the Church has inherited, fulfilled or replaced Israel’s covenant role. Its forms range from "fulfilment" (Israel’s hope finds its goal in Christ, with Jews welcome in the one Church) to punitive versions blaming Jews for Christ’s death.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/10/lab: Irenaeus: one householder of both covenants (c.180)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/10/tex: Against Marcion and the Gnostics, Irenaeus insists that the one Word gave both covenants and educated humanity step by step, so that the Law prepared for the gospel: a seed of later covenant and salvation-history theologies.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/11/tex: Augustine argues that Jews should be preserved as living witnesses to the Scriptures, a doctrine that shielded Jewish communities in Latin Christendom while still casting them as blind and subordinate.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/12/lab: Council of Mâcon makes the tithe obligatory (585)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/12/tex: Frankish bishops command payment of tithes under pain of excommunication; Charlemagne makes the tithe law (779). Medieval Christendom treats the Levitical tithe as binding church law, until tithe revolts, the French Revolution (1789) and 19th–20th-century commutations end it in most of Europe.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/13/lab: The "teaching of contempt": from Adversus Judaeos to expulsion (386–1543)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/13/tex: Chrysostom’s sermons against Judaizing Christians (386–87), the Rhineland massacres of the First Crusade (1096), Lateran IV’s distinctive dress (1215), blood-libel accusations, expulsions from England (1290) and Spain (1492), and Luther’s On the Jews and Their Lies (1543) show how anti-Jewish theology could become violence. Jules Isaac later named this "the teaching of contempt".
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/14/tex: For Luther the same Word speaks in two ways: the law commands, accuses and kills; the gospel promises and gives Christ. Confusing them produces either despair or self-righteousness. Moses binds Jews, not Gentiles, except where he restates natural law.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/15/lab: Bullinger: one eternal covenant of grace (1534)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/15/tex: Zurich’s Heinrich Bullinger writes the first treatise on the single covenant running from Adam and Abraham to Christ, grounding infant baptism (as circumcision’s successor) and a positive role for the Law in Christian life.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/16/lab: Melanchthon: the three uses of the law (1535)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/16/tex: Melanchthon’s Loci (1535) adds to the civil use (restraining evil) and the theological use (revealing sin) a "third use" guiding the regenerate. Calvin calls it the principal use.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/17/lab: Agricola: repentance comes from the gospel, not the law (1527–1540)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/17/tex: Johann Agricola contends that the law belongs "in the courthouse" and that true repentance is worked by the gospel of Christ’s suffering. Luther answers in six disputations and Against the Antinomians (1539): without the law, sin and grace alike are emptied of meaning. Agricola recants in 1540.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/18/lab: Calvin: the law as rule of grateful life (1559)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/18/tex: Calvin teaches one covenant in two administrations (Institutes 2.10–11): the ceremonies are abrogated in effect but not in significance, and the moral law, summarised in the Decalogue, guides believers in whom the Spirit reigns.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/19/lab: Formula of Concord: law and gospel, third use (1577)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/19/tex: Lutheran theologians confess that law and gospel must be carefully distinguished (Art. V) and that the law is to be preached to the regenerate as well (Art. VI), rejecting antinomianism.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/20/lab: Federal theology: covenant of works and covenant of grace (1585)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/20/tex: Reformed theologians (Ursinus, Fenner, Rollock, Perkins) frame all of history by a pre-fall covenant of works with Adam and a covenant of grace in Christ, administered under Law and gospel: one people of God in both testaments.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/21/lab: Anne Hutchinson accuses the ministers of a "covenant of works" (1636–38)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/21/tex: In Boston, Hutchinson’s followers charge that preachers who ground assurance in visible sanctification are preaching works. The colony’s leaders see antinomianism and private revelation; she is tried and banished.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/22/lab: Westminster Confession: covenants, law and the Christian Sabbath (1647)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/22/tex: Chapter 7 teaches a covenant of works and a covenant of grace "under the law" and "under the gospel"; chapter 19 holds that ceremonial laws are abrogated and judicial laws "expired together with the State of that people; not obliging any other now, further than the general equity thereof may require", while the moral law binds all; chapter 21 calls the Lord’s Day "the Christian Sabbath".
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/23/tex: Cocceius reads Scripture as an unfolding history of covenants, a forerunner of biblical theology; his followers’ looser view of the Sabbath sparks a long Dutch dispute with the Voetians.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/24/lab: Puritan Sabbatarianism: the Lord’s Day as Christian Sabbath
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/24/tex: From Nicholas Bownde (1595) to Westminster, Puritans teach that the fourth commandment is moral and perpetual, transferred to the first day: no work or recreation, the whole day given to worship and mercy. It shapes Scottish, English, American and Korean Protestant culture.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/25/lab: Marrow controversy: may Christ be freely offered to all? (1718–23)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/25/tex: Thomas Boston and the "Marrow men" defend the free offer of Christ and the believer’s freedom from the law as a covenant of works; the General Assembly condemns the Marrow (1720) as antinomian. Each side claims to be the faithful heir of Westminster.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/26/lab: Dispensationalism: Israel and the Church distinct (1830s)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/26/tex: J. N. Darby, and later the Scofield Reference Bible (1909), distinguish God’s earthly people Israel from his heavenly people the Church; the Mosaic law belonged to a past dispensation, and Israel’s national promises will be fulfilled literally in a future millennium.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/27/lab: Seventh-day Sabbath: keep the day God blessed (1650s; 1846)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/27/tex: Seventh Day Baptists (England, 1650s; Rhode Island, 1671) and later Seventh-day Adventists (Joseph Bates’ tract, 1846) argue that no Scripture transfers the Sabbath to Sunday. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church has long honoured both Saturday and Sunday, as affirmed under Emperor Zara Yaqob (c.1450).
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/28/lab: Christian Zionism and the State of Israel (1917–1948)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/28/tex: Dispensational and other philosemitic Protestants support a Jewish return to the land; British evangelical influence on the Balfour Declaration (1917) and American evangelical support after Israel’s founding (1948) make the theology of Israel a matter of world politics, contested by Palestinian Christians.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/29/tex: After the Holocaust, Christian self-examination (Seelisberg theses, 1947) leads Vatican II to reject the charge of collective Jewish guilt for Christ’s death and to affirm that the Jews remain dear to God. Many Protestant churches issue similar statements (e.g. the Rhineland Synod, 1980).
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/30/tex: R. J. Rushdoony and Greg Bahnsen argue that the moral and civil laws of Moses, including penal sanctions, remain binding unless the New Testament modifies them. Most Reformed bodies, including the faculty of Westminster Theological Seminary (Theonomy: A Reformed Critique, 1990), reject it as a misreading of the covenants and of WCF 19.4.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/31/tex: Jewish believers in Jesus form congregations that keep Sabbath, festivals and Jewish identity (Jews for Jesus, 1973; Messianic Jewish Alliance of America, renamed 1975). Mainstream Jewish bodies regard it as a form of Christianity; some Christians fear it rebuilds the wall of division.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/32/tex: Some theologians (James Parkes, Paul van Buren, Lloyd Gaston) hold that Jews are saved within God’s irrevocable covenant with Israel; others (R. Kendall Soulen, Mark Kinzer) reject supersessionism while confessing Christ as Israel’s Messiah, and envisage a "bilateral" church of Jews and Gentiles.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/33/tex: Craig Blaising, Darrell Bock and Robert Saucy see the kingdom inaugurated now, with Israel and the Church distinct but united in one unfolding plan; Christ already reigns on David’s throne.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/34/lab: New Covenant Theology and progressive covenantalism (1980s–2012)
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/34/tex: Mostly Baptist theologians argue that the whole Mosaic covenant, Decalogue included, ended at the cross; Christians live under "the law of Christ". Gentry and Wellum’s Kingdom through Covenant (2012) sets the biblical covenants in progressive sequence, fulfilled in Christ, between covenant theology and dispensationalism.
doctrines/covenant-law/flow/nodes/35/tex: Catholic teaching since 2015 ("The Gifts and the Calling of God Are Irrevocable") rejects supersessionism of the punitive kind and any institutional mission targeting Jews while affirming Christ as universal saviour; Orthodox churches generally retain a fulfilment view. Reformed and Presbyterian churches keep covenant theology; dispensationalism remains strong among American evangelicals, Pentecostals and their global partners; Lutherans teach law and gospel. Sunday worship is near-universal, with Seventh-day Adventists (over 20 million members) and Ethiopian Orthodox honouring the seventh day. Tithing is taught as binding in many Pentecostal, Adventist and Latter-day Saint communities and as a voluntary guide elsewhere.
